name: Carla Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am a senior field researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, political parties or government, and we do not sell anything or campaign. What you say is confidential. Can you tell me about a regular day at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am Carla Nakamura, 43, and I help with carpentry and general site work. I live with my partner and our two school-age children; I keep my framing square in the same pocket every day so I do not have to hunt for it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you do with the square and the other tools during a shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I carry boards, mark lengths and hold pieces while the carpenter fits them. I am still learning and have the carpenter check my square before I mark a frame; I like doing a task properly the first time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau: “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.”

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say a quicker list is useful if it brings the pieces we actually need. I would still measure against the wall before marking anything, because I am the one who has to fit it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Most of my work is lifting, marking and holding, so a small office change does not seem likely to replace my day. I still worry about money because we have less than a month saved for the mortgage and other bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep accepting the shifts on the schedule and ask the foreman what days are coming next. If pay were short, I would repair my old coat instead of replacing it right away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The software part feels small compared with what I do by hand. The hard part is that the mortgage stays fixed even if the site has fewer days for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you do when the material list does not match the room?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I stop before marking the board and ask the carpenter to look with me. A wrong measurement can cost us the piece and another trip for material.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What purchase at home could wait if work slowed down?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We could postpone replacing my coat if the seams still hold. I would not cut the children’s ordinary needs just to keep buying things for the house.

say: I would say **a quicker list** helps if it brings the pieces we need.
I would still **measure against the wall** before marking anything.
think: I do mostly **lifting and marking**, so a small office change seems limited for me.
I have **thin savings**, and the mortgage is a current worry.
do: Keep accepting **scheduled shifts** and ask what days are coming next.
Repair my **old coat** instead of replacing it if pay is short.
feel: **The software change** feels small, but the mortgage stays due if site days fall.
S0.quote: A wrong measurement can cost us the piece and another trip for material.
fieldNote: She sees little direct change to her **hands-on duties** in the mild scenario.
**Limited savings** make a fixed mortgage payment feel pressing during slow work.

steps.text: Keep accepting scheduled shifts and ask which days are next
Repair the old coat rather than replace it during a short-pay week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption: “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.”

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say a screen can prepare a list, but the crew should check the pieces when they arrive. I would learn a new tool if the foreman showed me it worked on our kind of job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AI may take the written notes I sometimes help with and schedule more deliveries by itself. I try a simple AI tool now and then at home, but I would need a plain demonstration before trusting it on a site task.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the foreman to show me the AI delivery screen on a small order and compare it with the paper sheet. If it proves accurate, I would use it for the next order and keep doing the fitting work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can try something once it has been shown to work. I would feel uneasy if learning it meant losing a paid shift or buying a device myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What result would convince you the new screen is useful?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want the items and lengths on screen to match the written plan and what we find at the wall. If the carpenter needs to correct it every time, it has not made the job simpler.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if you still did not trust its measurements?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep checking with my square and ask the carpenter before I mark the board. I do not want to blame a screen after we have already cut the wrong piece.

S1.quote: I do not want to blame a screen after we have already cut the wrong piece.
fieldNote: She uses AI occasionally but wants a **proven demonstration** for site work.
Her caution is about reliability and **unpaid time**, not a blanket rejection of tools.

steps.text: Learn the AI delivery screen with the foreman on a small order
Keep doing fitting work while checking the new process

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028: “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.”

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say thinking work changes first, and the robots come later. I would not tell my children or the crew that carpentry is safe just because the machines arrive on different dates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AI could do delivery notes and measurements that I sometimes help record by 2028. The physical work could last longer, but robots may take it by 2031, so I do not see the gap as a permanent shelter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Before 2028, I would ask the carpenter to teach me how he checks a frame and finishes a corner. In 2029, I would keep taking the shifts I can and avoid new household purchases until we see what my hours are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years gives me little time to get more skilled, but I would start with one task I can practise. I cannot promise my hours will stay steady, and that is what makes me anxious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children if your pay changed in 2028?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would explain that we may have to postpone a family outing and keep to the important bills. I would tell them we can talk about it together instead of hiding the change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you use the time before robots arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would use it to improve my fitting and finishing if a carpenter can teach me during work. I would still ask whether there are shifts before assuming the extra time pays our bills.

say: I would say **thinking work changes first**, before the later robot date.
I would not call **carpentry safe** just because the machines arrive at different times.
think: I think AI could do **delivery notes and measurements** by 2028.
I do not see the later robot date as **permanent shelter** for my job.
do: Ask the carpenter to teach me **frame checks** before 2028.
Avoid new household purchases in 2029 until I know **my hours**.
Take available **paid shifts** on site during 2029.
feel: **Two years** gives me little time to build more skill.
I feel anxious because I cannot promise **steady hours**.
S2.quote: I do not see the gap as a permanent shelter.
fieldNote: She understands **AI arrives before robots** and does not treat the delay as safety.
The **2029 plan** holds off purchases until her work hours are clearer.

steps.text: Practise frame checks and corner finishing with the carpenter before 2028
Delay new household purchases in 2029 until work hours are clearer
Take available paid site shifts during 2029

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031: “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.”

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say five years gives us time to practise more parts of the trade. I would not tell anyone that practice means the job will still be there after robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AI might do more of the measurements and written plans I help with by 2031. Robots could arrive around 2034, and then even the carrying and fitting may change, so I cannot assume my current duties last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for supervised practice on corners and fitting doors over the coming years. In 2032, I would ask local builders which skills they hire for before I paid for training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me time to improve without needing to rush into a risky course. I still feel anxious because our small savings would not carry us if I went many weeks without work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which fitting task would you want to practise first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would start with a door corner and ask the carpenter to watch me mark and trim it. I want to see the joint sit flat before I try the same task alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a course worth considering in 2032?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would need to know that a local builder uses the skill and has work connected to it. If the course only gives me a certificate without a clear job, I would not spend money we need for bills.

S3.quote: I want to see the joint sit flat before I try the same task alone.
fieldNote: She turns the warning time into **supervised finishing practice**.

steps.text: Practise door corners and fitting with a carpenter checking the work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036: “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.”

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say a decade gives people time to see what is changing and talk through choices. I would not tell a younger worker that later means the work is safe forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AI may take the measurements and written plans I help with by 2036, then robots could reach the site around 2039. My children will be older by then, and their needs may not be the same as the school costs we have now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep learning tasks on site while a skilled carpenter is still there to show me. In 2037, my partner and I would speak with our older child about study plans when the subject choices are near.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years gives me room to learn and notice which tasks employers still need. The mortgage and the children’s changing needs are happening along the way, so the warning does not remove today’s pressure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you make a study choice for the children now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would wait until the older one is choosing subjects and ask what they want to do. We can look at the options as a family when there is a real decision to make.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does ten years let you do that two years did not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could practise one task at a time and see how site work changes before spending on a course. I would still need to keep the household going while I watch for those changes.

say: I would say **a decade gives time** to watch and talk through choices.
I would not say **later means safe forever** for a younger worker.
think: I expect AI may take **measurements and written plans** by 2036, then robots may reach sites in 2039.
**My children** will be older, and their needs may differ from current school costs.
do: Keep learning **site tasks** while a skilled carpenter can show me.
Discuss **study plans** with my partner and older child in 2037, near their subject choices.
feel: **Ten years gives room** to learn and watch what employers still need.
The mortgage and my children’s **changing needs** still create pressure now.
S4.quote: We can look at the options as a family when there is a real decision to make.
fieldNote: She values a **longer period to prepare** without promising that site work stays safe.

steps.text: Keep learning site tasks through supervised practice

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me because I would have little time to improve before work changes. A carpenter who can teach me during paid shifts and steady work would help my family more than a course we cannot afford.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I am willing to learn when someone lets me try the task and checks the result. My partner and I need to keep the household steady while I learn, and no screen can make the mortgage wait.

theadlineQuote: No screen can make the mortgage wait.

biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** gives her little time to improve before work changes.
